texts.0: SP, due to failure to confirm station passage before starting the climbing turn, did not intercept and hold the published missed approach radial. The course indicator was allowed to run full deflection and the deviation exceeded 8 degrees while the aircraft kept diverging from the missed approach course. SP applied no correcting turn and the IP had to take control of heading to regain the radial before the holding fix.
texts.1: SP, due to late reference to the approach plate, delayed the turn to the missed approach radial and allowed the deviation to reach the 8 degree limit. SP corrected only after two verbal prompts from the IP indicating the course needle position, and the aircraft remained off the radial through most of the climb segment. No control input was needed from the IP, but the correction was neither self-initiated nor timely.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow initial turn rate after the missed approach point, let the aircraft drift off the published radial by more than 5 degrees, peaking short of the 8 degree limit. SP identified the course indicator displacement without prompting and applied a timely intercept turn that reestablished the radial before the level off. The deviation stayed within the 5 to 8 degree band and no IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP tracked the published missed approach radial accurately, keeping the deviation within 5 degrees throughout the climb. The intercept turn was started at the missed approach point and drift corrections were applied promptly, with wind correction refined as the aircraft climbed. Course guidance was cross checked against the approach plate and the aircraft arrived at the holding fix on radial.
texts.4: SP flew the missed approach radial with negligible deviation, holding the course indicator essentially centered and within about 2 degrees throughout the segment. The wind correction angle was set on the first correction and required no further adjustment, and the aircraft reached the holding fix precisely on course.
texts.marginal: SP kept the missed approach radial within standards, but the deviation stabilized close to the 5 degree limit and consistently on the downwind side, showing that the wind correction angle was set but never refined. Corrections were made in single large increments rather than small anticipatory inputs. SP is expected to reduce the residual radial error by trimming the correction angle early in the climb.

error_modes.label: Airspeed control during the missed approach

texts.0: SP, due to applying full power without a matching pitch increase, allowed the airspeed to build past the plus 15 knot tolerance during the initial climb, and later let it decay below the minus 10 knot limit while raising the nose to regain altitude. SP did not use the airspeed indicator as a primary reference during the transition and the trend was not arrested. The IP intervened on power and pitch to restore the target climb speed.
texts.1: SP, due to delayed power setting after the go around, let the airspeed decay to the minus 10 knot limit during the initial climb. SP restored the target speed only after the IP verbally called the airspeed twice, and the recovery was slow enough that the deviation persisted through the turn. The speed was eventually contained at the tolerance limit without any control input from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a coarse power advance at the missed approach point, allowed the airspeed to exceed the target by more than 10 knots but remain short of the plus 15 knot limit. SP detected the trend on the airspeed indicator and reduced power and adjusted pitch in time to bring the speed back into the primary band before the level off. No prompting or intervention was required.
texts.3: SP maintained the missed approach climb speed within plus 10 and minus 5 knots throughout the maneuver. Power was set promptly at the missed approach point and pitch was adjusted to hold the target speed, with small trim corrections applied as the configuration changed. Airspeed was included in the cross check at every stage of the climb.
texts.4: SP held the missed approach airspeed with negligible variation, staying within a few knots of the target from power application to level off. Power and pitch were coordinated so that no speed excursion developed during configuration change, and the aircraft was trimmed hands off at the climb speed.
texts.marginal: SP kept the missed approach airspeed within standards, but the speed repeatedly settled near the plus 10 knot edge of the primary band during the clean up, with corrections applied only after the deviation had developed. The pattern shows power being set by feel rather than confirmed against the airspeed indicator. SP is expected to anticipate the speed increase after gear and flap retraction and set the power more precisely.

texts_at.1: SP maintained the missed approach climb speed with the deviation settling at the minus 10 knot limit, due to delayed power setting after the go around. texts_at.2: SP maintained the missed approach climb speed with the deviation settling at about 12 knots above target, due to a coarse power advance at the missed approach point. texts_at.3: SP maintained the missed approach climb speed within plus 10 and minus 5 knots throughout the maneuver, due to one trim correction applied a beat after the configuration change rather than with it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply the trim correction together with every configuration change as consistently as the others.

texts_above.2: SP detected the trend on the airspeed indicator and reduced power and adjusted pitch in time to bring the speed back into the primary band before the level off, after the deviation had exceeded target by about 12 knots. Advancing power for the climb in a single measured action, rather than a coarse one, would keep that excursion smaller. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound climb-speed management.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the missed approach climb speed within plus 10 and minus 5 knots throughout the maneuver, with power set promptly at the missed approach point and pitch adjusted to hold the target speed. The only refinement available is to apply the trim correction together with every configuration change as consistently as the others. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed climb-speed management.
texts_above.4: SP held the missed approach airspeed with negligible variation, staying within a few knots of the target from power application to level off, with power and pitch coordinated so no speed excursion developed during configuration change. There is little left to refine; the aircraft is already trimmed hands off at the climb speed. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional climb-speed management.

error_modes.label: Timely initiation of the missed approach

texts.0: SP, due to continuation bias after a long approach with the runway environment expected at any moment, did not execute the missed approach at the missed approach point and continued the descent below minimums with no visual reference. The decision point was not called and no go around was initiated on SP initiative. The IP directed and then executed the missed approach to arrest the descent.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to abandon an approach that was nearly complete, held level at minimums past the missed approach point instead of initiating the climb. The missed approach was started only after the IP called the missed approach point, and the resulting delay put the aircraft near the limits of the published protected area with airspeed at the tolerance limit. No control input was required from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to attention remaining outside in search of the runway environment, initiated the missed approach several seconds after the missed approach point. SP recognized the delay without prompting, applied power and established the climb, and the resulting deviations stayed inside the primary tolerances. The maneuver was completed without prompting or intervention.
texts.3: SP identified the missed approach point on time and initiated the missed approach without hesitation, applying power and rotating to the climb attitude at the decision point. The decision was announced and the published procedure was flown from the correct point. Deviations remained within the primary tolerances throughout.
texts.4: SP executed the missed approach exactly at the published point with no hesitation, announcing the decision and transitioning to the climb in one continuous and correctly sequenced action. The timing was such that no deviation in course or airspeed developed at any stage.
texts.marginal: SP initiated the missed approach within standards, but only after a perceptible pause at the decision point that suggests SP was still weighing whether the approach could be salvaged. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to outstanding decision discipline at the missed approach point.

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate preflight review of the published missed approach, did not know the climb altitude, the turn point or the holding fix, and flew a self invented track instead of the charted procedure. The sequence of actions was not executed IAW the Techniques and Procedures Manual and MAIP, and the aircraft departed the protected airspace of the procedure. The IP had to take control and fly the published missed approach.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete approach briefing, confused the order of the published missed approach steps and started the turn before reaching the charted turn point. The correct sequence was recovered only after the IP prompted with the charted altitude and fix, and the radial deviation reached the tolerance limit before the aircraft was reestablished. texts.2: SP, due to hesitation in recalling the published climb altitude, executed the missed approach steps out of the ideal order and had to reread the plate during the climb. SP identified the discrepancy without prompting and reordered the actions in time, keeping course and airspeed inside the secondary band. The procedure was completed correctly and without intervention.
texts.3: SP executed the published missed approach procedure in the correct sequence and without misapprehension, flying the charted climb, turn point and holding fix IAW the Techniques and Procedures Manual, MAIP and Local Area Procedures. The steps were recalled from the briefing and confirmed against the plate. All parameters remained within the primary tolerances.
texts.4: SP flew the published missed approach flawlessly and from memory, with every step in the correct order and confirmed against the plate without interrupting the instrument cross check. The climb, turn and holding entry were executed as charted with no hesitation and no deviation of consequence.
texts.marginal: SP flew the published missed approach correctly, but needed to consult the plate at each step rather than executing from a briefed plan, which slowed the sequence and left little margin before the turn point. error_modes.label: Configuration clean up within airspeed limits

texts.0: SP, due to omitting the standardized clean up sequence, left the aircraft in the approach configuration during the climb and then retracted the gear and flaps out of order and outside the published airspeed limits. The configuration change was not IAW the standardized procedures and the airspeed excursion that followed exceeded the plus 15 knot tolerance. The IP intervened to manage the configuration and restore the climb speed.
texts.1: SP, due to fixation on course guidance, delayed the clean up so that the aircraft climbed in the approach configuration and the airspeed fell to the minus 10 knot limit. The gear and flaps were retracted only after the IP called for the configuration change, and the sequence was completed late although within the placard speeds. No control input was needed from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a rushed power application, called for the clean up slightly out of the standardized order and retracted the flaps before confirming a positive rate of climb. texts.3: SP cleaned up the aircraft configuration according to the standardized procedures, retracting gear and flaps in the correct order after a positive rate of climb was established and within the published airspeed limits. texts.4: SP cleaned up the configuration precisely to the standardized sequence, timing each retraction so that no airspeed or pitch excursion developed. Gear and flap indications were confirmed without interrupting the instrument cross check, and the aircraft was trimmed at the climb speed immediately after the clean up.

error_modes.label: Pitch, power and altitude control in the go around transition

texts.0: SP, due to advancing the power without setting the climb attitude on the attitude indicator, did not arrest the descent at the missed approach point and the aircraft continued below minimums before any climb developed. The pitch and power inputs were not coordinated and the airspeed excursion exceeded the tolerance while the aircraft failed to reach the published climb altitude. The IP took control to establish the climb.
texts.1: SP, due to an under set climb attitude, established only a shallow climb after the missed approach point and levelled off well below the published missed approach altitude. The correct attitude and altitude were achieved only after repeated verbal direction from the IP, and the airspeed reached the tolerance limit during the correction. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly aggressive rotation at the go around, allowed the pitch to overshoot the climb attitude and the aircraft to balloon above the intended climb profile with airspeed above the primary band. SP detected the attitude and speed trend on the instruments and reset pitch and power in time, containing the deviations short of the tolerance limits without prompting or intervention.
texts.3: SP transitioned smoothly to the go around, applying power and setting the climb attitude on the attitude indicator in one coordinated action, arresting the descent immediately at the missed approach point. The climb was stabilized and levelled at the published missed approach altitude with all parameters inside the primary tolerances. Trim was used to hold the climb attitude.
texts.4: SP executed the go around transition with negligible deviation, arresting the descent at the missed approach point and holding the climb attitude and the published altitude essentially exactly. Pitch, power and trim were coordinated so that no altitude overshoot or speed excursion occurred at any point.
texts.marginal: SP arrested the descent and climbed to the published altitude within standards, but the level off was reached with a small overshoot each time and the aircraft was flown to altitude by control pressure rather than by trim. All parameters stayed within tolerance. SP is expected to lead the level off earlier and trim off the residual pressure to steady the climb profile.

Course, airspeed and altitude were all allowed to diverge beyond the published tolerances without being detected, and SP lost awareness of the aircraft position relative to the missed approach fix. The IP intervened to restore the flight path and the instrument scan.
texts.1: SP, due to task saturation at the missed approach point, narrowed the instrument scan to the navigation display and did not include airspeed and altitude until the IP called them out. The deviations reached the tolerance limits before the scan was restored, and awareness of the position relative to the holding fix was regained only through IP prompting. No control input was needed from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a temporarily narrowed scan while managing power and configuration, omitted the airspeed indicator for several seconds and allowed the speed and course to drift past the primary band. texts.3: SP maintained a complete instrument cross check throughout the missed approach, including attitude, airspeed, altitude and course guidance while managing power and configuration. texts.4: SP sustained a full and evenly distributed instrument cross check through every phase of the missed approach, so that deviations were caught at the trend stage and never developed into measurable errors. Awareness of the aircraft position relative to the missed approach fix and holding pattern was continuous and correct at all times.

No parameter left tolerance. SP is expected to keep the scan rate constant through the clean up so deviations are caught at the trend stage.

texts_above.3: SP maintained a complete instrument cross check throughout the missed approach, including attitude, airspeed, altitude and course guidance while managing power and configuration, with position awareness relative to the missed approach fix continuous. error_modes.label: Power reduction once at the targeted missed approach pitch

texts.0: SP, due to leaving the PCL at MAX after the targeted 10 to 15 degrees Nose-High attitude had been reached, never reduced power as the technique requires and let the pitch run well above the targeted band. The airspeed decayed past the minus 10 knot tolerance while SP flew a steepening attitude in IMC without reference to the EADI. The excessive pitch produced disorientation and the climb was never stabilized, so the IP intervened on the PCL and the stick to reset the missed approach attitude.
texts.1: SP, due to not reducing power once at the targeted pitch, allowed the nose to rise above 15 degrees Nose-High and the airspeed to fall to the minus 10 knot limit. Power was retarded only after the IP called the attitude and then the airspeed, and the pitch was reset late in the climb segment. The deviation was contained at the tolerance limit and no control input from the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power reduction after reaching the targeted pitch, let the attitude drift a few degrees above the 10 to 15 degrees Nose-High band and the airspeed fall more than 5 knots below target, short of the minus 10 knot limit. SP recognized the pitch increase on the EADI without prompting and retarded the PCL in time to restore the climb attitude and speed. No intervention was required.
texts.3: SP set the missed approach attitude at 10 to 15 degrees Nose-High and reduced power as necessary once at the targeted pitch, so no excessive pitch developed. Attitude was held on the EADI and the airspeed remained within plus 10 and minus 5 knots of the target throughout the climb. The aircraft was trimmed at the climb attitude before the clean up.
texts.4: SP reached the targeted 10 to 15 degrees Nose-High attitude and reduced power in the same smooth movement, so the pitch stabilized without any overshoot and the airspeed varied by only a few knots. No disorientation cue was allowed to develop and the attitude was held essentially exactly on the EADI throughout the climb.
texts.marginal: SP reduced power after reaching the targeted pitch and kept all parameters within standards, but each reduction came a beat late and the attitude settled at the upper edge of the 10 to 15 degrees Nose-High band with the airspeed near the minus 5 knot edge. The attitude was recovered by control pressure rather than by setting a known power value. SP is expected to anticipate the power reduction as the targeted pitch is reached so the climb stabilizes without an initial pitch excursion.

texts_at.1: SP reduced power once at the targeted pitch with the nose rising above 15 degrees Nose-High and airspeed falling to the minus 10 knot limit before the reduction was applied, due to power being retarded only after the attitude and then the airspeed were called. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce power the instant the targeted pitch is reached, not after a verbal call.
texts_at.2: SP reduced power once at the targeted pitch with airspeed falling to about 7 knots below target before the reduction settled the climb, due to the reduction coming a beat after the targeted pitch was reached. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to anticipate the power reduction as the targeted pitch is reached rather than after it.
texts_at.3: SP set the missed approach attitude at 10 to 15 degrees Nose-High and reduced power as necessary once at the targeted pitch, holding airspeed within plus 10 and minus 5 knots, due to the reduction being timed a fraction later than ideal on one occasion. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to time the reduction the same way on every missed approach as consistently as the others.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the pitch increase on the EADI without prompting and retarded the PCL in time to restore the climb attitude and speed, after airspeed had fallen more than 5 knots below target. Anticipating the power reduction as the targeted pitch is reached, rather than after it, would keep that deviation smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound power-and-pitch coordination on the go around.
texts_above.3: SP set the missed approach attitude at 10 to 15 degrees Nose-High and reduced power as necessary once at the targeted pitch, so no excessive pitch developed and airspeed remained within plus 10 and minus 5 knots. error_modes.label: Verifying the climb on VSI and altimeter before raising gear and flaps

texts.0: SP, due to raising the gear and flaps without first checking the VSI and the altimeter to verify the climb, retracted the configuration while the aircraft was still settling after the missed approach point. The altimeter continued to unwind and the airspeed fell past the minus 10 knot tolerance as the drag was removed with no climb established. The IP intervened on pitch and power to arrest the descent and establish the climb.
texts.1: SP, due to calling for the clean up on the sound of the power application rather than on a verified climb, moved the gear handle before the VSI and altimeter had been checked. The IP directed SP twice to confirm the climb indications, and the airspeed reached the minus 10 knot limit before the climb was positively established. No control input from the IP was needed.
texts.2: SP, due to a hurried sequence at the missed approach point, started the clean up with only a glance at the VSI and without confirming the altimeter trend. SP interrupted the retraction on its own initiative, verified the climb on both instruments and completed the configuration change, holding the speed excursion short of the primary tolerance. No prompting or intervention was required.
texts.3: SP checked the VSI and the altimeter to verify the climb before raising the gear and flaps, so the configuration was changed only with a positive rate established. Both indications were included in the cross check and called before the retraction, and airspeed stayed within plus 10 and minus 5 knots of the target. The clean up followed the standardized sequence.
texts.4: SP verified the climb on the VSI and altimeter and only then raised gear and flaps, with the check completed without any interruption of the instrument cross check. The retraction produced no perceptible pitch or airspeed excursion and the climb continued precisely on the target profile.
texts.marginal: SP verified the climb before the clean up and stayed within standards, but the VSI was accepted alone on two occasions and the altimeter trend was confirmed only after the gear was already travelling. The indications were correct and the sequence was completed properly. SP is expected to confirm both the VSI and the altimeter before moving the gear handle rather than after.

texts_at.1: SP verified the climb before raising gear and flaps, with airspeed reaching the minus 10 knot limit before the climb was positively confirmed, due to calling for the clean up on the sound of the power application rather than on verified indications. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check the VSI and altimeter before moving the gear handle on every occasion, not after.
texts_at.2: SP verified the climb before raising gear and flaps, with the speed excursion held short of the primary tolerance, due to starting the clean up with only a glance at the VSI on one occasion. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm both the VSI and the altimeter trend before every retraction as consistently as the others.
texts_at.3: SP checked the VSI and the altimeter to verify the climb before raising gear and flaps, holding airspeed within plus 10 and minus 5 knots, due to the altimeter trend being confirmed a beat later than the VSI on one occasion. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the VSI and the altimeter together on every occasion rather than in sequence.

texts_above.2: SP interrupted the retraction on its own initiative, verified the climb on both instruments and completed the configuration change, holding the speed excursion short of the primary tolerance, after starting the clean up with only a glance at the VSI. Confirming both the VSI and the altimeter trend before every retraction would prevent that interruption from being needed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to solid climb-verification discipline.
texts_above.3: SP checked the VSI and the altimeter to verify the climb before raising gear and flaps, so the configuration was changed only with a positive rate established and airspeed stayed within plus 10 and minus 5 knots. The only refinement available is to confirm the VSI and the altimeter together rather than in sequence. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to well-developed climb-verification discipline.
texts_above.4: SP verified the climb on the VSI and altimeter and only then raised gear and flaps, with the check completed without interrupting the instrument cross check and no perceptible pitch or airspeed excursion, about 3 knots at most. There is little left to refine; the climb is already confirmed before the configuration is touched. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to outstanding climb-verification discipline.

error_modes.label: False sensation of climb produced by acceleration

texts.0: SP, due to accepting the false sensation of climb produced by the acceleration at the go around instead of confirming the attitude on the EADI, flew the aircraft on seat of the pants cues and relaxed the back pressure. The nose was lowered while SP believed the aircraft was climbing steeply, and the airspeed exceeded the plus 15 knot tolerance with no climb established. SP did not resolve the conflict between the sensation and the instrument indications and the IP took control to set the missed approach attitude.
texts.1: SP, due to the strong climb sensation generated by the acceleration, held a pitch attitude below the targeted band and let the airspeed build to the plus 15 knot limit before the EADI was believed. The attitude was reset only after the IP repeatedly called the pitch and the vertical velocity indication. The deviation was held at the tolerance limit without any control input from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to the acceleration cue at the missed approach point, initially flew a shallower attitude than the targeted 10 to 15 degrees Nose-High and allowed the airspeed to rise more than 10 knots above target, short of the plus 15 knot limit. SP cross checked the EADI and the VSI, rejected the false sensation without prompting and reset the climb attitude in time. No intervention was required.
texts.3: SP disregarded the false climb sensation produced by the acceleration and flew the missed approach on the instruments, setting and holding the targeted Nose-High attitude on the EADI. The pitch was confirmed against the VSI and altimeter rather than against physical cues and the airspeed remained within plus 10 and minus 5 knots of target. The climb was stable from the missed approach point.
texts.4: SP flew the entire missed approach on instrument indications with no trace of the acceleration illusion in the control inputs. The targeted attitude was set and held on the EADI, cross checked against the VSI and altimeter, and pitch and airspeed showed only negligible variation throughout the climb.
texts.marginal: SP flew the missed approach within standards but the pitch was consistently set slightly low at the moment of the power application, with the attitude corrected upward once the VSI was read, showing that the acceleration cue was influencing the initial input. All deviations stayed inside the tolerances. SP is expected to set the attitude directly on the EADI at power application and treat the climb sensation as an unreliable cue.

texts_at.1: SP disregarded the false climb sensation with airspeed building to the plus 15 knot limit before the EADI was believed, due to the strong climb sensation generated by the acceleration holding a pitch attitude below the targeted band. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to set the attitude on the EADI at power application before any sensation can influence it.
texts_at.2: SP disregarded the false climb sensation with airspeed rising to about 12 knots above target before the correct attitude was set, due to the acceleration cue at the missed approach point initially producing a shallower attitude than targeted. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to cross-check the EADI against the VSI the instant the acceleration is felt, not after the speed has already built.
texts_at.3: SP disregarded the false climb sensation produced by the acceleration and flew the missed approach on the instruments, holding airspeed within plus 10 and minus 5 knots, due to the attitude being confirmed against the VSI a beat later than ideal on one occasion. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm the attitude against the VSI with the same timing on every occasion.

texts_above.2: SP cross checked the EADI and the VSI, rejected the false sensation without prompting and reset the climb attitude in time, after airspeed had risen more than 10 knots above target. Cross-checking the EADI against the VSI the instant the acceleration is felt, rather than after the speed has built, would keep that excursion smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady disorientation-resistant technique.
texts_above.3: SP disregarded the false climb sensation produced by the acceleration and flew the missed approach on the instruments, setting and holding the targeted Nose-High attitude on the EADI with airspeed remaining within plus 10 and minus 5 knots. The only refinement available is to confirm the attitude against the VSI with the same timing on every occasion. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to consistently accurate disorientation-resistant technique.
texts_above.4: SP flew the entire missed approach on instrument indications with no trace of the acceleration illusion in the control inputs, the targeted attitude set and held on the EADI and pitch and airspeed showing only negligible variation, about 3 knots. There is little left to refine; the climb sensation is already treated as unreliable from the first moment. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary disorientation-resistant technique.

error_modes.label: Smooth advance of the PCL to MAX at the missed approach point

texts.0: SP, due to slamming the PCL forward to MAX instead of advancing it smoothly, produced a large yaw and roll excursion that was not countered with rudder at the missed approach point. The aircraft departed the published radial by more than 8 degrees while SP chased attitude and heading together, and the airspeed excursion exceeded the tolerance as well. The IP intervened on rudder and stick to stabilize the climb and regain the course.
texts.1: SP, due to an abrupt power application at the go around, allowed the yaw to displace the aircraft off the missed approach radial to the 8 degree limit before any rudder correction was made. The correction followed two verbal prompts from the IP on trim and heading, and the aircraft remained off course through the early climb. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a rapid rather than smooth advance of the PCL to MAX, generated a yaw excursion that pushed the radial deviation past 5 degrees but short of the 8 degree limit. SP identified the course displacement and applied rudder and rudder trim on its own initiative, reestablishing the radial before the level off. No prompting or intervention was required.
texts.3: SP advanced the PCL smoothly to MAX at the missed approach point and countered the yaw with coordinated rudder as the power came up. The aircraft stayed within 5 degrees of the published radial through the power application and the climb, and rudder trim was reset for the new power setting. The transition was made without any heading chase.
texts.4: SP advanced the PCL to MAX with a single smooth movement and matched it with rudder so that no yaw excursion was visible on the instruments. The radial deviation stayed close to zero through the power application and the aircraft was trimmed for the climb immediately afterwards.
texts.marginal: SP advanced the PCL to MAX and stayed within standards, but the movement was quicker than the technique calls for and the resulting yaw carried the radial deviation close to the 5 degree limit before rudder was applied. The correction was made and the course was regained. SP is expected to lead the power application with rudder and advance the PCL smoothly so no course excursion develops.

texts_at.1: SP advanced the PCL to MAX with the radial deviation settling at the 8 degree limit before rudder was applied, due to an abrupt power application at the go around producing a yaw excursion before any correction was made. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to lead the power application with rudder rather than applying rudder after the yaw develops.
texts_at.2: SP advanced the PCL to MAX with the radial deviation settling at about 6 to 7 degrees before it was corrected, due to a rapid rather than smooth advance of the PCL generating a yaw excursion. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to advance the PCL smoothly rather than rapidly on every missed approach as consistently as the others.
texts_at.3: SP advanced the PCL smoothly to MAX at the missed approach point and countered the yaw with coordinated rudder as the power came up, holding radial deviation within 5 degrees, due to the rudder trim reset being made a beat later than ideal on one occasion. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to reset rudder trim together with the power application on every occasion.

texts_above.2: SP identified the course displacement and applied rudder and rudder trim on its own initiative, reestablishing the radial before the level off, after the deviation had passed 5 degrees but stayed short of the 8 degree limit. Advancing the PCL smoothly rather than rapidly on every missed approach would keep that deviation smaller. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable yaw-control technique.
texts_above.3: SP advanced the PCL smoothly to MAX at the missed approach point and countered the yaw with coordinated rudder as the power came up, staying within 5 degrees of the published radial through the power application and the climb. The only refinement available is to reset rudder trim together with the power application on every occasion. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good yaw-control technique.
texts_above.4: SP advanced the PCL to MAX with a single smooth movement and matched it with rudder so no yaw excursion was visible on the instruments, with the radial deviation staying close to zero, about 1 degree, through the power application. There is little left to refine; the aircraft is already trimmed for the climb immediately afterward. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior yaw-control technique.

error_modes.label: Setting power and pitch for target climb airspeed at 140 to 180 KIAS

texts.0: SP, due to never making the climb speed setting in the 140 to 180 KIAS window, left the PCL at MAX and the climb attitude unchanged after the clean up. The aircraft accelerated through the window unchecked and the airspeed exceeded the plus 15 knot tolerance on the target climb speed, with no power or pitch adjustment attempted. The IP intervened on power and pitch to establish the target climb airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to a late recognition of the 140 to 180 KIAS window, set power and pitch for the climb only after the aircraft had accelerated to the plus 15 knot limit on the target climb speed. The setting was made in response to repeated airspeed calls from the IP and the speed was contained only at the tolerance limit. No control input from the IP was needed.
texts.2: SP, due to setting power before adjusting pitch as the aircraft passed through the 140 to 180 KIAS window, allowed the airspeed to rise more than 10 knots above the target climb speed but short of the plus 15 knot limit. SP noted the trend on the airspeed indicator and coordinated pitch with the new power setting in time, returning the speed to the primary band. No intervention was required.
texts.3: SP set power and pitch for the target climb airspeed as the aircraft passed 140 to 180 KIAS, so the acceleration after the clean up was captured at the correct point. The resulting speed stayed within plus 10 and minus 5 knots of the target through the climb and the aircraft was trimmed at that setting. The transition from the go around attitude to the climb attitude was smooth.
texts.4: SP made the climb setting precisely inside the 140 to 180 KIAS window, coordinating power and pitch so the aircraft settled on the target climb airspeed without overshoot. The speed varied by only a few knots for the rest of the climb and the aircraft was trimmed hands off at the climb attitude.
texts.marginal: SP set power and pitch for the target climb airspeed inside the 140 to 180 KIAS window and remained within standards, but the setting was made at the top of the window each time and the speed peaked near the plus 10 knot edge before settling. The setting itself was correct and the climb was stabilized. SP is expected to begin the power and pitch change earlier in the window so the target climb speed is captured without an overshoot.

texts_at.1: SP set power and pitch for the target climb airspeed with the deviation settling at the plus 15 knot limit before the setting was made, due to a late recognition of the 140 to 180 KIAS window that let the aircraft accelerate to the limit first. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to recognize the 140 to 180 KIAS window on the first pass through it, not after acceleration is well established.
texts_at.2: SP set power and pitch for the target climb airspeed with the deviation settling at about 12 knots above target, due to power being set before pitch was adjusted as the aircraft passed through the window. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to coordinate power and pitch together as the window is entered rather than in sequence.
texts_at.3: SP set power and pitch for the target climb airspeed as the aircraft passed 140 to 180 KIAS, holding the resulting speed within plus 10 and minus 5 knots of target, due to the setting being made at the top of the window rather than as it opened. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make the setting at the same point in the window on every occasion.

texts_above.2: SP noted the trend on the airspeed indicator and coordinated pitch with the new power setting in time, returning the speed to the primary band, after the deviation had risen more than 10 knots above target. Coordinating power and pitch together as the window is entered, rather than in sequence, would keep that deviation smaller. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to assured climb-speed capture technique.
texts_above.3: SP set power and pitch for the target climb airspeed as the aircraft passed 140 to 180 KIAS, so the resulting speed stayed within plus 10 and minus 5 knots of target and the aircraft was trimmed at that setting. The only refinement available is to make the setting at the same point in the window on every occasion. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to precise climb-speed capture technique.
texts_above.4: SP made the climb setting precisely inside the 140 to 180 KIAS window, coordinating power and pitch so the aircraft settled on the target climb airspeed without overshoot, varying by only about 3 knots for the rest of the climb. There is little left to refine; the aircraft is already trimmed hands off at the climb attitude. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate climb-speed capture technique.

error_modes.label: Airspeed schedule on vectors for an additional approach

texts.0: SP, due to disregarding the airspeed schedule for vectors after the missed approach, held a speed of its own choosing instead of 150 to 200 KIAS and did not slow to 160 KIAS on radar base. The deviation from the required speed exceeded the plus 15 knot tolerance and the aircraft arrived at the final approach course too fast to configure. The IP intervened on power to bring the aircraft back to the required pattern airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to not planning the deceleration from the 200 KIAS radar downwind speed, entered radar base at the plus 15 knot limit on the required 160 KIAS. The speed was reduced only after the IP twice called for the base leg airspeed, and the aircraft remained fast through the turn to final. No control input from the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a late power reduction leaving radar downwind, allowed the speed on radar base to exceed the required 160 KIAS by more than 10 knots but stay short of the plus 15 knot limit. SP recognized the excess on the airspeed indicator and reduced power in time to stabilize at the required speed before the intercept. No prompting or intervention was required.
texts.3: SP flew the required airspeed schedule after the missed approach, maintaining 150 to 200 KIAS on vectors, 200 KIAS on radar downwind and slowing to 160 KIAS on radar base. Each speed was held within plus 10 and minus 5 knots and the changes were anticipated so no rushed corrections were needed. The aircraft was stable and in trim at every stage.
texts.4: SP flew the post missed approach vectors precisely on the required schedule, holding 200 KIAS on radar downwind and 160 KIAS on radar base with negligible variation. The decelerations were led by an early power reduction so each target speed was captured without overshoot and without any pitch excursion.
texts.marginal: SP flew the required airspeed schedule on vectors within standards, but each deceleration was started late and the speed settled near the plus 10 knot edge before stabilizing on the target. The correct speeds were eventually established at every stage. SP is expected to plan the deceleration ahead of the base turn so the required speed is set on entering the leg rather than during it.

texts_at.1: SP flew the airspeed schedule on vectors with the deviation settling at the plus 15 knot limit on the required 160 KIAS before the reduction was made, due to not planning the deceleration from the 200 KIAS radar downwind speed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to plan the deceleration from the downwind speed before radar base is reached, not on entering it.
texts_at.2: SP flew the airspeed schedule on vectors with the deviation settling at about 12 knots above the required 160 KIAS, due to a late power reduction leaving radar downwind. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to reduce power the instant radar downwind is left rather than partway down radar base.
texts_at.3: SP flew the required airspeed schedule after the missed approach, maintaining 150 to 200 KIAS on vectors, 200 KIAS on radar downwind and slowing to 160 KIAS on radar base, holding each speed within plus 10 and minus 5 knots, due to one deceleration being started a beat later than ideal. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to start every deceleration at the same point as consistently as the others.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the excess on the airspeed indicator and reduced power in time to stabilize at the required speed before the intercept, after the deviation had exceeded the required 160 KIAS by more than 10 knots. Reducing power the instant radar downwind is left, rather than partway down radar base, would remove most of that excess. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent airspeed-schedule discipline.
texts_above.3: SP flew the required airspeed schedule after the missed approach, maintaining 150 to 200 KIAS on vectors, 200 KIAS on radar downwind and slowing to 160 KIAS on radar base, with each speed held within plus 10 and minus 5 knots and changes anticipated so no rushed corrections were needed. The only refinement available is to start every deceleration at the same point as consistently as the others. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined airspeed-schedule discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew the post missed approach vectors precisely on the required schedule, holding 200 KIAS on radar downwind and 160 KIAS on radar base with negligible variation, about 3 knots, with decelerations led by an early power reduction so each target speed was captured without overshoot. There is little left to refine; every deceleration is already anticipated rather than rushed. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to faultless airspeed-schedule discipline.
